summary: Defines how PCEP encodes objective functions, which are the optimization criteria used when computing traffic engineering label switched paths, such as minimum cost or widest path. A client can then tell the PCE what kind of best path it wants.

plainLanguage.summary: A path computation server chooses a route by some goal, such as the cheapest or the least crowded path. RFC 5541 defines how a client asks for a particular goal, how the server reports which one it used, and how the server says which goals it supports. It defines six common goals as standard codes.

subtitle: How a PCEP client tells a path computation server what 'best path' means, and the server replies.

tldr.problem: When a Path Computation Element computes a traffic engineering path, there are many ways to define the best path (cheapest, least loaded, widest), and PCEP had no way to ask for a particular one or to learn which ones a PCE supports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an OF-List TLV in the Open message so a PCE can advertise its objective functions, an OF object in request and reply messages to ask for and report one, and a new RP flag to ask the PCE which one it used. It defines six objective functions and four new metric types.
tldr.outcome: A client can require or merely prefer an objective function, and a PCE can reject, substitute or report one. Other documents may define more objective functions.

facts.label: Objective function codes
facts.value: 1 to 6 (MCP, MLP, MBP, MBC, MLL, MCC)

today: RFC 5541 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2009. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It complements RFC 5440, the base PCEP specification.

sections.title: Why Objective Functions Are Needed
sections.content:
In the Path Computation Element architecture (RFC 4655), a Path Computation Element (PCE) computes paths for Traffic Engineered Label Switched Paths from a network graph and a set of constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) sends it requests, and the two communicate using PCEP, defined in RFC 5440.

Choosing among candidate paths needs an optimization criterion, called an objective function. Some apply to one request on its own, such as the shortest constrained path using the IGP metric. Others apply to a set of synchronized requests, such as minimizing the aggregate bandwidth consumption of all paths. Some optimize a single metric and others a set of metrics.

This RFC extends PCEP so that a PCE can advertise a list of supported objective functions and so that request and reply messages can carry the objective function. It defines the six objective functions that RFC 4657 requires PCEP to support.
sections.plainLanguage: There is more than one way to pick the best route, like shortest or least crowded. The client and the server need a shared way to say which one they mean.

sections.title: Discovering Supported Objective Functions
sections.content:
A PCE may advertise what it supports using a new optional OF-List TLV, carried in the OPEN object of an Open message during PCEP session setup. The TLV uses the standard PCEP TLV layout: a 2-octet type 4, a 2-octet length and a value that is a list of 2-byte objective function code points. The length is N * 2 for N objective functions. The TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment, and the padding is not counted in the length.

The OF-List TLV MUST NOT appear more than once in an OPEN object. If it does, the session MUST be rejected with error type 1, error value 1 (PCEP session establishment failure, reception of an invalid Open message). If the TLV is absent, that means only that there is no information about supported objective functions. A peer that does not recognize the TLV silently ignores it, as RFC 5440 specifies.

The RFC notes that OSPF- and IS-IS-based PCE discovery (RFC 5088, RFC 5089) covers only a few generic parameters, while more detailed parameters such as objective functions are better discovered over PCEP itself.
sections.plainLanguage: When two programs first say hello, the route-planner can hand over a list of the goals it knows how to chase. If it hands over no list, the other side simply does not know what it supports.

sections.title: The OF Object and Where It Goes
sections.content:
The new OF object has Object-Class 21 and Object-Type 1. Its body holds a 2-byte OF Code, a 2-byte Reserved field (set to zero on transmission, ignored on receipt) and optional TLVs that may be defined later to carry objective function parameters.

A PCC may include the OF object in a PCReq (path computation request) to say which function it wants. A PCE may include it in a PCRep (path computation reply) to say which function it used, and it MAY be attached to a negative reply, one carrying a NO-PATH object.

A function applied to a set of synchronized requests MUST be carried just after the corresponding SVEC object and MUST NOT be repeated for each elementary request. A function applying to one individual request MUST follow the RP object for which it applies. A metric applied to a set of synchronized requests also follows the SVEC object.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a small record naming the chosen goal. When one goal covers a whole group of trips, it is recorded once for the group rather than repeated for each trip.

sections.title: How a PCE Answers a Request
sections.content:
The P bit in the object's common header decides whether the request is a requirement. If the P bit is set in the OF object, the objective function is mandatory and the PCE MUST use it. If the P bit is clear, the function is only desired, so the PCE SHOULD apply it when supported but MAY choose another according to local capabilities and policies.

  • If the objective function is unknown or unsupported and the P bit is set, the PCE MUST send a PCErr with error type 3 or 4 and error value 4, and discard the request. If the P bit is clear, the PCE SHOULD apply another (default) objective function.
  • If the function is not permitted by policy and the P bit is set, the PCE MUST send a PCErr with error type 5 (policy violation) and error value 3, objective function not allowed.
  • If the request sets the new Supply OF on response flag (bit 24 of the RP object) and policy permits, the PCE MUST include an OF object in the reply reporting the function it used. If policy does not permit, it MUST send a PCErr with error type 5 and a new error value defined under policy violation.

A legacy PCE ignores the unknown flag and replies without an OF object; the PCC then decides for itself whether to accept or discard the reply.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can mark a goal as a must or just a preference. A must is obeyed or refused; a preference lets the server choose and, when asked, say which goal it followed.

sections.title: The Six Objective Functions and Four New Metrics
sections.content:
The RFC defines three functions for a single path and three for a set of synchronized requests. It uses a simple model: a network of N links, a path P of K links, a link metric M(L), a path cost C(P) that is the sum of its link metrics, a residual bandwidth r(L) and a maximum reservable bandwidth R(L).

  • Single path: Minimum Cost Path (code 1) minimizes C(P). Minimum Load Path (code 2) minimizes the largest fraction of reserved bandwidth on any link of the path. Maximum residual Bandwidth Path (code 3) maximizes the smallest residual bandwidth on the path.
  • Synchronized set: Minimize aggregate Bandwidth Consumption (code 4), Minimize the Load of the most loaded Link (code 5) and Minimize the Cumulative Cost of a set of paths (code 6).

For the METRIC object, PCEP already had TE metric, IGP metric and hop count, which apply to one request. This RFC adds four types for a set of synchronized requests: type 4 aggregate bandwidth consumption, type 5 load of the most loaded link, type 6 cumulative IGP cost and type 7 cumulative TE cost. They can bound a result or request a computation in a PCReq, or report a computed metric in a PCRep.
sections.plainLanguage: Some goals are about one trip: the cheapest, the least crowded, the widest. Others are about a whole group of trips together, such as using the least total capacity across all of them.

sections.title: Registries and Code Points
sections.content:
IANA manages a 16-bit "PCE Objective Function" registry shared by the OF object and the OF-List TLV. Code 0 is reserved. Codes 1 through 1023 are assigned by IETF Review, 1024 through 32767 are First Come First Served, and 32768 through 65535 are for Private Use. Codes 1 to 6 are assigned to MCP, MLP, MBP, MBC, MLL and MCC.

The RFC also records the OF object (class 21, type 1), the OF-List TLV (type 4), the RP flag bit 24 and metric types 4 to 7. Two new error values under error type 5 (policy violation) are added: value 3, objective function not allowed, and value 4, OF bit of the RP object set.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list keeps track of which number means which goal, so everybody uses the same numbers. Some number ranges are for public assignment and some are reserved for private use.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
Nothing here changes message flows or adds new messages, so the PCEP security mechanisms of RFC 5440 still apply and automatically secure the OF object. If a PCEP message is vulnerable because security is not used, the OF object could be part of an attack, but the RFC considers it likely that other objects offer far more significant ways to attack a PCE or PCC.

For management, it MUST be possible to enable or disable objective function discovery and to configure a default objective function. An implementation SHOULD allow a list of authorized objective functions on a PCE. Implementations need not support every function defined in this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal record travels in the same protected envelope as everything else in the protocol, so it gets the same protection. Operators can also decide which goals a server is allowed to follow.
